questions.title: Why did the Seventh Circuit review the consent finding only for clear error instead of deciding de novo?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the standard of review on appeal here. The opinion says the district court's finding of voluntary consent and the scope of that consent are reviewed for "clear error." But whether a search violates the Fourth Amendment usually sounds like a legal question. Why isn't the court independently deciding for itself whether Lisa's words and conduct amounted to valid consent? Is the idea that voluntariness and scope are treated as fact-heavy determinations, even though they apply constitutional doctrine?

questions.title: How can Lisa's second 'Okay' count as consent when she had already said she preferred the officers not enter?
questions.question_body: The facts that are tripping me up are: Officer Kizer first asked if he could enter, and Lisa said, "um ... I'd prefer you not." Then later, after he said, "I'm sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure" the kids were okay, she said, "Okay," and opened the door. I'm not sure how courts treat this kind of sequence. Does the initial refusal matter a lot, or can a later statement fully override it? Also, how do courts decide whether the later response is a real change of mind versus submission to pressure?

questions.title: When does a police statement that they 'need' to come inside become coercive under Bumper and Schneckloth?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Coleman's best argument was Officer Kizer's use of the word "need," but the court still found no coercion under the totality of the circumstances. I'm trying to understand the doctrinal line here. In Bumper, consent isn't valid if it's just acquiescence to a claim of lawful authority. So why wasn't "we almost need to come inside" treated as effectively telling Lisa that entry was going to happen anyway? Is the key difference that Kizer phrased it as concern and not as an assertion of legal authority, or is there more to it?

questions.title: What exactly was the objective scope of Lisa's consent once the officers entered the home?
questions.question_body: The court says the officers stayed within the scope of consent because their purpose was to check on the children and determine whether Coleman posed a danger. But I'm unsure how broad that makes the consent in practical terms. If Lisa only consented to the officers coming in to see whether the kids were okay, why did that also authorize a sweep of the home to find Coleman in a separate bedroom? Is that because a reasonable person would understand child-welfare checking in a domestic violence situation to include locating the allegedly violent person, or because the consent implicitly covered officer-safety steps too?

questions.title: Why didn't the court analyze exigent circumstances if this was a reported domestic violence emergency with children inside?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that the government alternatively argued exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery, but the court declined to reach those issues because it found valid consent. I'm wondering whether, on these facts, exigent circumstances might actually have been the cleaner theory. The officers had a 911 report of threats to kill, possible children at risk, and an unknown location of the suspect inside the home at 4:00 a.m. Is there some reason appellate courts prefer not to decide alternative Fourth Amendment exceptions once one exception clearly applies?

questions.title: How did the later search warrant avoid 'fruit of the poisonous tree' problems if the entry had been unlawful?
questions.question_body: I understand that because the court found the initial entry lawful by consent, the later warrant and gun recovery were fine. But I'm trying to think through the alternative. The officers learned from the children after entering that Coleman had pointed a gun and threatened Lisa, and that information helped them get the search warrant. If the entry had been illegal, would the warrant automatically be tainted as fruit of the poisonous tree? Or could the government still have saved the evidence through inevitable discovery, an independent source theory, or by showing enough untainted facts already existed before entry?

questions.title: Why was Lisa's role as a co-occupant enough for consent without discussing Georgia v. Randolph or objecting occupants?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Matlock and says a third party with common authority can consent, which makes sense because Lisa lived there too. But I was expecting some discussion of cases about one occupant objecting to a search. Coleman was apparently somewhere in the house when Lisa let the officers in. Does it matter that he wasn't asked first, or that he didn't object before the officers found him? I'm confused about when a present co-occupant's potential objection defeats another occupant's consent and when it doesn't.
